title: Define it
hook: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, as it is (Meditations 3.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was only now. Your line was only this: the one moment anyone lives. Today a week closes.

A worry rarely arrives in plain words. It arrives as a cloud. Something about money. Something about that test result. Something about the way she said goodnight. It's big and blurry and fills the room. Now try writing it down in one flat sentence, the way a clerk would. Sometimes the cloud shrinks the moment it has edges. Marcus Aurelius used this trick on himself, and wrote down how it works. Today: define it.
screen: `A WORRY ARRIVES AS A CLOUD.` → `WRITE IT LIKE A CLERK.` → `DEFINE IT.`

segments.voice: Book three's eleventh entry calls this one more aid to add to the others. Always make a definition, or a description, Marcus writes, of whatever presents itself to your mind. See what it is in substance, stripped bare, whole, and tell yourself its name and the names of the parts it's made of. His point is that what upsets us is often less the thing than the coat we put on it. A late bill becomes I'm failing at life. A curt email becomes they're about to fire me. Defining strips the coat off. A late bill is a piece of paper asking for an amount by a date. That may still be a problem, but now it's one you can see. Then he asks of each thing: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last, and what does it ask of me? Gentleness, courage, truth, faithfulness, simplicity? A defined thing points to a response. A cloud just points to dread. Nothing so enlarges the mind, he says, as being able to examine everything that happens methodically and truly. Look at what this week has built. While I can. Could I say it. Nothing better. Keep faith. Judge carefully. Only this. And now, as it is. Seven short lines, each small enough to say in one breath.
screen: `MAKE A DEFINITION OF EACH THING.` · `STRIP OFF THE COAT.` · `WHAT IS IT, WHAT DOES IT ASK OF ME?` · `SEVEN SHORT LINES.` · then, large: `AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Bring up one worry that's been sitting with you, and let it be a cloud for a moment. Then describe it in one flat sentence, as a clerk would, with no adjectives and no predictions: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last? Last, ask Marcus's question, what does it ask of me, and notice its size now.
Define it. Marcus's method: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, name it and its parts, and ask what it asks of you. Today's word.
Your line: as it is. A thing with edges is a thing you can meet. A full week, done.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.11 by writing a worry down in one plain sentence, naming what it is and what it asks of them, before deciding how to respond.

fork.setup: on the drive to work, your car starts making a new grinding noise. your mind fills with storm clouds. what fits 3.11?
options: imagine every way it could go wrong.
describe it plainly: a new noise, from the front, when braking.
turn up the radio and ignore it.
fork.reveal: Marcus defines the thing bare: a noise, with a place and a time. what it asks of you, for now, is a call to a mechanic and some patience.

Marcus Aurelius.meaning: Roman emperor and Stoic who wrote notes to himself

stripped bare.meaning: seen as it is, without the coat of fear we add

definition.meaning: for Marcus, a plain description of what a thing is

notes: 3.11 paraphrased: make a definition or description of the thing presented, to see what it is in substance, in its nudity, as a whole; tell yourself its name and the names of its components; nothing is so productive of magnanimity as to examine methodically and truly all that presents itself; ask what it is, what it is composed of, how long it will last, and what virtue it needs from me (gentleness, manliness, truth, fidelity, simplicity, contentment). Confirm.
